ety.text: From Middle English putten, pitten, pytten, puten, poten, from Old English putian, *pūtian ("to push, put out"; attested by derivative putung (“pushing, impulse, instigation, urging”)) and potian (“to push, thrust, strike, butt, goad”), both from Proto-West Germanic *putōn, from Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab”), which is of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bud- (“to shoot, sprout”), which would make it cognate with Sanskrit बुन्द (bundá, “arrow”), Lithuanian budė, and budis (“mushroom, fungus”).
Unknown. Perhaps related to Welsh pwt, itself possibly borrowed from English butt (“stub, thicker end”).

senses.d: To physically place (sth or sb swh).
ex: She put her books on the table.
The police put him in a cell.

senses.d: To place in abstract; to attach or attribute; to assign.
ex: The government put restrictions on vehicle imports.
I put £100 on the winning horse.

senses.d: To bring or set (into a certain relation, state or condition).
ex: Put your house in order!
He is putting all his energy into this one task.

senses.d: To express (something in a certain manner).
ex: When you put it that way, I guess I can see your point.
To put it bluntly, he's an idiot.

senses.d: To set before one for judgment, acceptance, or rejection; to bring to the attention.
ex: I put it to you, Sir, that you are a thief and a liar.
to put a question; to put a case

senses.d: To set as a calculation or estimate.
ex: They have put the cost of repairs at around £10 million.

senses.d: To steer; to direct one's course; to go.
ex: to put to sea
His fury thus appeased, he puts to land.

senses.d: To sell (assets) under the terms of a put option.
ex: He got out of his Procter and Gamble bet by putting his shares at 80.

senses.d: To throw with a pushing motion, especially in reference to the sport of shot put. (Do not confuse with putt.)
ex: He put the shot out beyond the 20-metre mark.

senses.d: To play a card or a hand in the game called “put”.
The act of putting; an action; a movement; a thrust; a push.
ex: the put of a ball
The Stag's was a Forc'd put, and a Chance rather than a Choice.

senses.d: A fellow, especially an eccentric or elderly one; a duffer.
ex:
Queer Country-puts extol Queen Bess's reign,
And of lost hospitality complain.
Any number of varlet to be had for a few ducats and what droll puts the citizens seem in it all!
And Mrs. Penny-a-hoist Pim, said Mr. Gorman. That old put, said Mr. Nolan.
